 Republican Ron Johnson, who earlier this week called Social Security a "Ponzi scheme", has put forward a new bill to help address the program's longstanding funding issues. The Wisconsin Senator and Chairman of the Senate Budget Committee introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act on Wednesday, which would require the Treasury to transfer money to the Social Security trust funds to help pay benefits for more than 70 million Americans. The combined funds are currently scheduled to run out of money in 2032, and without a solution, only 78 percent of scheduled benefits will be payable. His proposal comes just a couple of days after he told Fox News that Social Security was a "legal Ponzi scheme." A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that uses funds from new investors to pay existing ones. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program that uses dedicated tax revenue from current workers to pay recipients, and does not conceal how its funds are used. “It’s a Ponzi scheme,” Johnson said. “You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money.” He later said during a Senate Budget Committee hearing on Wednesday that his comments on shutting down Social Security had been "imprecise" and that he is "not proposing shutting down Social Security." Newsweek has contacted Johnson's office for comment via email outside of regular working hours. What's In The Bill? Johnson's bill, one of several recently proposed to help shore up the Social Security trust funds, proposes transferring money from the federal government's general fund to the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund once its assets are insufficient to meet monthly benefit payments. Social Security benefits are funded by dedicated payroll taxes, which pays for benefits issued currently. Any surplus revenue is held in trust funds that are invested in special U.S. Treasury securities. But since 2021, the program has been paying out more than it receives from these taxes, meaning the trust fund reserves are being used to make payments. The most recent Social Security Trustee's report found the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund, which pays retirement benefits and benefits to eligible family members of deceased workers, will run out toward the end of 2032. At that point, benefits would be funded solely through incoming payroll taxes, triggering an automatic cut of around 22 percent unless Congress acts. The dwindling funds have been attributed to a large number of Baby Boomers retiring in recent years and lower birth rates, meaning there are less workers to pay taxes to meet the payment obligations. Maya MacGuineas, president of the nonpartisan fiscal watchdog Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), told Newsweek that she disagreed with Johnson's description of it being a Ponzi scheme. "It is not a Ponzi scheme, but it is based on a lot of outdated premises," MacGuineas said. "The Chairman was right to ring the warning bell, but his newest idea to fund the system with general revenues is perhaps the worst solution out there because it would explode the national debt." The CRFB has predicted the bill, if enacted, could add $190 trillion to the national debt over 75 years. Fixing Social Security Johnson's bill is one of two that have proposed using primarily other revenue streams to prop up Social Security funding. Other Senators and Representatives from both sides of the aisle have submitted bills, most of which propose raising taxes to bolster revenue. Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Val Hoyle have put forward the Social Security Expansion Act, which would apply payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000, along with taxes on investment gains. Currently, only $184,500 of earnings are subject to the dedicated Social Security payroll tax. The Social Security 2100 Act, introduced to the Senate by Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal and in the House by Democrat John Larson during the summer, proposes similar tax increases for high earners and investment income. A different proposal has been pushed by Republican Senator Bill Cassidy and Democratic Senator Tim Kaine, who have proposed creating a new, separate investment fund for Social Security. "We borrow 1.5 trillion dollars, we put it in an investment fund separate from Social Security trust fund, put it into the broader economy, and allow it to grow over six decades," Cassidy told CBS. "At which point it pays for up to 70 percent of what we need to cover the debt for Social Security." What Happens Next The Stop Scaring Seniors Act has been referred to the Senate Finance Committee. Correction: 11/21/2026, 06:05 ET. An earlier version of this article misrepresented the time frame in which OASI is projected to run out. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.
